covers.quote: The word ‘dove’ is the past tense of ‘dive’ in American English.

examples.note: Example of dived as past tense of dive

parts.quote: Bystanders dived into the creek to help the drowning swimmer.

rules.quote: In Australian English, write ‘dived’ to use the past tense of the verb ‘to dive’.
rules.violation_condition: the word ‘dove’ used as the past tense of ‘dive’
rules.why: G-4 states the rule directly for past tense of dive.

examples.note: Example using 'for all intents and purposes'

parts.quote: The paperwork may take a few weeks to come through but, for all intents and purposes, you are hired.

rules.quote: The correct expression is ‘for all intents and purposes’, meaning ‘in every practical sense’.
rules.why: Clear rule defining the correct fixed expression against the common error.

covers.quote: The exception is a court decision; write this as ‘judgment’.

parts.quote: You can speak to one of our counsellors without fearing judgement.
Please cite the High Court’s most recent judgment in the issues paper.

rules.violation_condition: the spelling ‘judgment’ when not referring to a court decision
when: Except when referring to a court decision, which is written as ‘judgment’.
rules.why: G-2 consolidates the preference for 'judgement' with its legal exception under when.

parts.quote: He completed his master degree last year.

examples.note: Specific qualification using 'Master of [area of study]'

parts.quote: Having a Master of Arts helped her gain the promotion.
The university offered several master degrees to postgraduate students.

rules.quote: Use ‘master degree’. When referring to a specific qualification, use ‘Master of [area of study]’.
rules.violation_condition: using ‘masters degree’ or ‘master’s degree’ instead of ‘master degree’
when: When referring to a specific qualification, use ‘Master of [area of study]’.
rules.why: Prescribes standard term 'master degree' and specific title format.

covers.quote: Use ‘program’ for the titles of new programs based on government policy. Use ‘programme’ only when it is part of the formal name of an existing program.

parts.quote: One of the most challenging aspects of our work is designing programs that can be implemented quickly.

examples.note: Exception for formal name of existing program

parts.quote: The Prescription Shopping Programme lets medical practitioners check their patients’ prescription histories.

rules.quote: Use ‘program’ rather than ‘programme’, including for computer programs.
rules.violation_condition: the spelling ‘programme’ when not part of the formal name of an existing program
when: Use ‘programme’ only when it is part of the formal name of an existing program.
rules.why: G-2 consolidates general spelling preference with proper noun exception.

covers.quote: ‘Irregardless’ is likely a combination of the words ‘irrespective’ and ‘regardless’. It is not accepted as standard Australian English.

parts.quote: Our aim is for all staff to have access to this training, regardless of location.
The following instructions will work regardless of which mobile platform you use.
These are interesting times but we must carry on regardless.

rules.why: Direct prohibition of 'irregardless' in favour of 'regardless'.

parts.quote: If I had known we were over budget, I would have changed the scope of the contract.
This would’ve spared us a lot of stress
At the very least, we would of avoided the overspend.

rules.quote: Always write ‘would have’ or the contracted form ‘would’ve’. ‘Would of’ is incorrect.
